definition: A state of temporary pause, when something is set aside for now but may start again later.
example: The town's plan for a new library was held in abeyance until the budget recovered.
nuance: Unlike cancellation or abolition, abeyance means a pause, not an end: the matter is expected to resume someday.
prompt: A museum's renovation stalls while engineers inspect cracks in the building's foundation.
options: The renovation was held in abeyance until the engineers finished their report.
The director showed abeyance to the engineers by bowing deeply as they entered.
With the renovation in abeyance, workers hammered away on the new gallery all week.
The museum had such abeyance of donations that it added two wings.
reasons: The project is paused for now and will continue once the inspection is done.
This confuses the word with obeisance, a gesture of respect, not a pause.
Busy hammering means work is going on, which contradicts a suspended project.
This mixes the word up with abundance; it has nothing to do with having plenty.

practice.prompt: A family postpones a long-planned road trip after their car breaks down.
options: The children knelt in abeyance before their grandmother to thank her for the map.
Putting the trip in abeyance meant they erased it from their plans for good.
Their road trip stayed in abeyance until the mechanic could replace the engine.
Their trip was in abeyance, so they left at dawn and drove four hundred miles.
reasons: Kneeling in thanks describes obeisance, a look-alike meaning humble respect.
Dropping something forever is cancellation; the word implies it may come back.
The trip is on hold, with a clear chance of going ahead once the car is fixed.
Setting off and driving far means the trip is happening, not paused.
